name: The Focus
purpose: Select useful information, shift attention as the task changes, and build a practical preparation and refocus plan.
case_title: Jordan returns to the next free throw
case:
Jordan is a fictional Grade 10 basketball player. During open play, Jordan needs to notice the ball, defenders and available teammates. At the free-throw line, the task changes. Jordan has practised a brief setup: find the line, release extra shoulder tension, look at the chosen rim target and use the cue “smooth.”

At the last school practice, Jordan missed a shot after a rushed setup. Jordan then thought, “I always fail when people watch,” looked toward a spectator and missed the teammate's signal for the next drill. The coach observed the rushed setup and offered a chance to practise it again. One missed cue does not tell us its only cause. In this case, Jordan's own account supplies additional evidence about attention.

The next practice includes a planned interruption: the drill order changes before Jordan's turn. You will help Jordan prepare, notice the new demand and select a useful next cue. Treat the case as fictional. An academic parallel is preparing to explain a graph after a classroom presentation order changes. An artistic parallel is returning to an agreed musical entry after an interruption. You may use one of these settings throughout your work.
opening: Describe Jordan’s task before a free throw and during open play. What useful information changes between those moments?

lessons.title: What attention does
lessons.intro: Choose useful information, stay with it, and notice when the task changes.
lessons.goal: I can explain selection, sustaining attention and shifting using a specific task.
lessons.before: Picture a performer who has more information available than they can use at once.
lessons.core:
## Attention gives the task a place to start
A school gym contains voices, moving people, floor markings and a scoreboard. A player cannot treat every detail as equally important. **Attention** concerns how information is selected and used. **Concentration** means keeping attention with what matters for the task. It does not mean blocking out everything around you.

Four useful actions are selecting, sustaining, noticing and shifting. **Selecting** means choosing information. **Sustaining** means staying with it long enough to do the job. **Noticing** means detecting a relevant change. **Shifting** means moving attention when another cue becomes more useful. These actions often work together rather than appearing as four separate stages.

## Select according to the demand
Ask, “What decision or action is needed now?” A player deciding where to pass needs different information from a player taking a free throw. A presenter explaining a graph needs to attend to its key relationship. Reading every word on a slide may compete with that job.

Useful information is **task-relevant**: it helps the current action. A distraction pulls attention toward something less useful at that moment. The same sound can serve either role. A musician may need a partner's entry cue, while an unrelated conversation adds nothing to the next phrase. Relevance depends on the task, not just whether the information is inside or outside the performer.

## Capacity is limited
Trying to hold many instructions at once can make the next action unclear. “Watch everyone, remember every correction and never make a mistake” gives attention several competing jobs. A shorter cue can help organize a familiar action. It cannot supply a skill the person has not learned.

Limited capacity does not mean a person is unable to learn. It means the plan should decide what deserves attention now. During learning, there may be time to examine a movement carefully. During a familiar performance, one well-understood cue may be more usable than a list of corrections.

## Notice before explaining a miss
A missed cue is an observation. Its cause is a further question. The cue might have been unclear, unexpected or hidden. The performer might have been attending elsewhere. Ask what was noticed, what the person was trying to do and whether the instructions changed.

A useful plan does not demand perfect concentration. It identifies the relevant information, provides a way to notice drift and names a return point. The next topics give more precise language for that plan.
lessons.worked:
Mina is preparing a short class presentation. Before speaking, Mina checks the graph's main relationship. During the explanation, Mina notices a classmate's question. Looking at the graph was useful first; listening becomes useful next.

A phone notification is less relevant to either task. The plan is to silence it during preparation, then use “main relationship” as the opening cue. This supports selection and sustaining attention. It does not mean Mina must ignore a relevant question to prove concentration.
lessons.application: What information matters in this moment? Identify one distraction and explain why it is less useful now.
lessons.label: Select information for the next action
expected: State the exact action or decision.
Identify one relevant cue and one less useful distraction.
Explain why the distinction fits this moment.

checks.prompt: A performer stays with the agreed rhythm through a short musical phrase. Which attention action is most directly shown?
choices: Shifting to an unrelated stimulus.
Sustaining attention on a useful cue.
Measuring their total mental capacity.
checks.feedback: The performer remains with the rhythm long enough to complete the phrase. The description does not measure overall capacity.

checks.prompt: A player misses a teammate’s signal. What information is most useful before explaining why?
choices: The final score alone.
A permanent label for the player’s concentration.
What the player was attending to and whether the signal was clear.
checks.feedback: Several explanations are possible. The task, signal and performer’s account help distinguish them.

lessons.support: Use three questions: What am I doing? What information helps? What has changed? A distraction is information that competes with the present task. A cue that was useful a moment ago can become less useful after the task changes.

lessons.title: Four ways to focus
lessons.intro: Describe attention by its width and its direction.
lessons.goal: I can distinguish the four attention quadrants in a clearly stated moment.
lessons.before: Separate how much information is used from where that information comes from.
lessons.core:
## Two questions form four quadrants
The attention framework associated with **Robert Nideffer** combines two dimensions. **Width** describes whether attention is broad or narrow. **Direction** describes whether it is internal or external. Broad attention takes in several pieces of information. Narrow attention selects a specific cue. Internal attention concerns thoughts or bodily sensations. External attention concerns information in the surroundings.

Combine the dimensions to name four quadrants: broad-external, broad-internal, narrow-internal and narrow-external. These labels describe the focus used in a moment. They do not divide students into permanent kinds of people. A useful performer can change focus when the demand changes.

## Broad-external: scan the surroundings
A basketball player scans the ball, defenders and available teammates before a pass. Several external cues matter together. That is a broad-external example. Broad does not mean noticing everything equally. It means gathering enough relevant information to read the play.

A recreational hiker checking the route, group position and nearby conditions offers another example. The situation determines which details belong in the scan. Looking around without a purpose may simply add distractions.

## Broad-internal: consider information and options
During a pause, a player considers the coach's plan, the available options and an earlier pattern in the game. Those thoughts are internal, and several pieces are being considered. This is broad-internal attention.

A student organizing the argument for a presentation also uses several internal ideas. Analysis can be useful when there is time for it. The question is whether the current moment calls for planning or for carrying out the next prepared action.

## Narrow-internal: one thought or sensation
During a safe pause, a performer briefly checks whether their shoulders are unnecessarily tense. The focus is internal and specific. Recalling one short cue can also be narrow-internal. This is different from repeatedly scanning every possible bodily sensation.

An internal check should have a clear purpose and an ending. After the check, the performer returns to information needed for the task. A long search for a perfect feeling may compete with preparation.

## Narrow-external: one useful outside cue
A free-throw shooter looks at a chosen part of the rim. A musician watches the conductor's entry signal. Each selects a specific external cue. Narrow attention is useful here because the next action has a precise target.

No quadrant is always best. A narrow target that helps a free throw may hide useful information during open play. Judge the focus against the task rather than calling broad, narrow, internal or external attention automatically good or bad.
lessons.worked_title: Describe the moment, not the whole athlete
lessons.worked:
Jordan is waiting at the free-throw line. During a safe pause, Jordan briefly notices extra shoulder tension. This is narrow-internal attention: one bodily cue. Jordan then looks at the chosen rim target, which is narrow-external.

The framework describes two moments in the same routine. It does not prove that Jordan belongs to an “internal type.” Once play resumes, a wider scan may be needed. The explanation must include the task and timing of each focus.
lessons.application: Choose the focus needed at a stated moment and explain the evidence supporting your choice.
lessons.label: Match a quadrant to a moment
expected: Name the task and moment.
State width and direction separately.
Use the actual information in the case to justify both.

checks.prompt: During a pause, a player compares several possible strategies in their thoughts. Which quadrant fits?
choices: Broad-internal.
Narrow-external.
Broad-external.
checks.feedback: The information consists of several internal options. A pause provides a setting where considering them may fit.

checks.prompt: During open play, Jordan needs to see defenders and available teammates before passing. Which focus fits?
choices: Narrow-internal attention to one breath.
Broad-external attention to the relevant play.
Narrow-external attention only to the scoreboard.
checks.feedback: Several external cues are needed for the pass. The other choices leave important task information out.

lessons.support: Use two labels before combining them. Is the performer using one cue or several? Is that information in their thoughts/body or in the surroundings? Then explain whether that focus fits the action. The quadrant name alone is not the whole answer.

lessons.title: Shift as the task changes
lessons.intro: Use a change in the task as a signal to change attention.
lessons.goal: I can explain a sequence of attention shifts and the trigger for each change.
lessons.before: Bring forward the four quadrants; no single quadrant is the permanent target.
lessons.core:
## A useful focus can become an old focus
During open play, Jordan scans defenders and teammates. A whistle stops the play. The coach gives a short instruction. Later, Jordan takes a free throw. Holding exactly the same focus across these moments would not meet all three demands.

An **attention shift** is a change in the information selected. It may change width, direction or both. A plan is stronger when it names what triggers the shift. “Focus better” is vague. “When the whistle stops play, listen for the instruction” links an event to a useful response.

## Scan, plan, check and target
One teaching sequence begins with a broad-external scan of the situation. During a suitable pause, broad-internal attention may help the performer consider options. A brief narrow-internal check may identify an unnecessary tension signal. Narrow-external attention can then select the target for a precise next action.

This sequence is an example, not a ritual everyone must complete. Some tasks need fewer shifts. Others require repeated scanning during action. The performer should not add an internal check if it distracts from information needed for safety or execution. The task decides the sequence.

## Give every transition a reason
For each moment, name the demand, the information and the trigger. A passing decision calls for information about space and teammates. A planned break permits discussion. An aiming attempt calls for the established target. The transition matters because the information needs have changed.

A musician may listen broadly to the ensemble, consider an adjustment during a pause, briefly recall the agreed count and then watch a specific entry cue. A presenter may scan the audience for a question, think through a response, choose the relevant example and point to one part of a graph. Neither situation needs a sport setting to use the framework.

## Avoid two common traps
The first trap is staying with the last mistake. The result has happened, but attention remains on a judgment instead of the next demand. A brief factual review can be useful later. During the next action, use a cue that belongs to that action.

The second trap is changing focus without a reason. Constantly checking body sensations, the score and other people's reactions can create competing jobs. A prepared transition can reduce unnecessary searching, while remaining flexible when new information matters.

## Check whether the shift served the task
Record what the performer intended to notice and what they actually noticed. Did the cue make the next action clearer? Was important information missed? One result does not prove that the shift caused success or failure. Use the observation to decide what to keep, clarify or practise again.
lessons.worked:
Jordan scans the ball and available teammates during play. When the whistle sounds, the task becomes listening to the official rather than continuing the pass. At the free-throw line, Jordan uses the familiar setup and chosen target.

A useful plan names those transitions. It does not instruct Jordan to repeat all four quadrants while the ball is live. Attention shifts because the task changes, not because completing a four-box sequence earns a better result.
lessons.application: Describe how attention changes from scanning, to planning, to a brief body check, to the next target.
lessons.label: Explain the transitions
expected: Give a clear setting for each moment.
Name the information and quadrant.
Explain what signals each shift and where a step might be unnecessary.

checks.prompt: What makes an attention-shift plan more usable?
choices: Using the same quadrant for every situation.
Changing focus whenever any thought appears.
Naming the task change that triggers a new focus.
checks.feedback: A trigger connects the shift to an actual demand. It helps the performer know when the previous cue no longer fits.

checks.prompt: A planned solo becomes a duet just before rehearsal. What should change first?
choices: Identify the partner cues and revise the attention sequence.
Keep the solo plan unchanged to protect consistency.
Add more internal checks regardless of the new task.
checks.feedback: The duet introduces information about another performer. The plan needs to account for those cues rather than preserve an outdated sequence.

lessons.support: Write a three-column sequence: moment, information, trigger. For example: open play—teammates and space—scan while deciding; whistle—official’s instruction—stop and listen; free throw—chosen target—use the practised setup. Explain why the information changes.

lessons.title: Observe without judging yourself
lessons.intro: Replace a judgment about the whole person with information about an attempt.
lessons.goal: I can use an attributed coaching framework without treating it as a measured equation.
lessons.before: Recall the difference between an observed action and a claim about identity.
lessons.core:
## A mistake and its interpretation are different
“The ball landed short” describes a result. “I am useless” judges the whole person. The second statement gives little direction for the next attempt. It may also compete with information the performer needs. A useful response starts with what happened and what can be examined.

**Nonjudgmental observation** means describing a relevant feature without turning it into a verdict on personal worth. It does not mean pretending the attempt was correct. A performer can acknowledge a missed shot and ask for feedback without calling themselves a failure.

## Gallwey's Inner Game framework
Timothy Gallwey uses the coaching framework **performance = potential − interference**. Here, interference means influences that get in the way of using a learned skill. Excessive self-criticism or trying to control every small movement may be examples in a particular case.

Treat the equation as an organizing idea, not arithmetic. This lesson does not measure a student's potential or subtract a numerical amount of interference. Many other features of a task matter, including instruction, preparation, skill and conditions.

The framework uses **Self 1** for the telling, judging voice and **Self 2** for the performer using learned capabilities. These are model labels. They are not two brain structures or two separate people inside a learner. Their purpose is to help discuss how commentary can compete with execution.

## Analysis still has a place
A beginner may need a demonstration and careful attention to a movement. A performer may need to analyse an error at a sensible break. “Trust the skill” cannot replace learning a missing skill or listening to accurate feedback.

The distinction concerns timing and purpose. During practice, a coach can explain one correction. During a familiar attempt, the performer may use one understood cue rather than rehearse a long list of technical instructions. Afterwards, the action can be reviewed again.

## Move from judgment to evidence
Use three parts: observation, possible explanation and next action. Keep the explanation open when the evidence is limited. “My setup was shorter than usual; I may have rushed; I will use the agreed setup cue next time” is more useful than “I always choke.”

A school example works the same way. “I left out the evidence for my claim” identifies something to revise. “I am bad at every subject” does not. A realistic observation can support a clear correction while preserving the fact that the work needs improvement.

The aim is not to remove every unhelpful thought. Notice when a thought pulls attention away, then return to a task-relevant action. Review the pattern without grading yourself on whether your mind felt perfectly quiet.
lessons.worked_title: Keep the error; change the conclusion
lessons.worked:
After the missed free throw, Jordan says, “I always fail when people watch.” The coach observed a rushed setup. A stronger statement is, “I shortened my setup on that attempt. I will use the familiar preparation cue before the next shot.”

This does not promise the next shot will score. It identifies an action Jordan can try and review. If the setup remains unclear, instruction and practice are needed. A positive phrase alone would not fix that gap.
lessons.application: Turn a global judgment into a specific observation and next action. Explain why the new wording is more useful.
lessons.label: From judgment to observation
expected: Identify the global judgment.
Keep the observed error without exaggerating it.
Choose a relevant action and explain the limit of the conclusion.

checks.prompt: How should Self 1 and Self 2 be described in this lesson?
choices: Two anatomical brain systems measured by the game.
Labels in Gallwey’s coaching framework.
Permanent personality categories.
checks.feedback: They are labels used to discuss commentary and learned execution. The lesson does not identify separate anatomical systems.

choices: Nothing went wrong, so no correction is needed.
I am not a natural performer and cannot improve.
My entry was late; I will practise the agreed count and check it.
checks.feedback: The response acknowledges a specific error and names a next action. It avoids both denial and a global judgment.

lessons.support: Describe the attempt as though you were reporting a short video: what could be seen or heard? Then add one relevant adjustment. Gallwey’s framework helps organize that discussion; it does not calculate a learner’s ability or remove the need for feedback.

lessons.title: Cue words and anchors
lessons.intro: Give attention a short, meaningful place to return.
lessons.goal: I can select a cue and anchor that fit a particular task.
lessons.before: A cue must connect to an action the performer understands and has practised.
lessons.core:
## A cue is a reminder, not a complete lesson
A **cue word** is a short word or phrase used to direct attention or support action. It works best when the performer already understands its meaning. “Smooth” may remind Jordan of a practised release. For someone who has not learned that action, the word may be too vague.

A useful cue is short enough to use in the available moment. “Change your feet, shoulders, hands and timing” gives several competing instructions. During learning, those features may need separate explanation. During a familiar attempt, select the cue most relevant to the identified task.

## Instructional and motivational purposes
An **instructional cue** directs technique, timing or relevant information. “See the target,” “steady count” and “main evidence” can serve that purpose in different settings. The phrase should tell the performer something useful about what to do.

A **motivational cue** supports effort or commitment. “Keep going” or “commit to this phrase” can serve that purpose. It should not pressure someone to ignore a real need for support. A more intense phrase is not automatically a better one.

Classify a cue by the job it does, not only its wording. “Finish” could remind a musician to sustain a final note or encourage a student to complete a familiar task. The explanation of its purpose makes the distinction clear.

## An anchor gives attention a return point
An **anchor** is a chosen cue, sensation or action that helps the performer return to the task. A rim target, an agreed musical count or a key word on a speaking card can be an anchor. The performer should know when to use it and what comes next.

An anchor is not a lucky object that guarantees a result. It is also not necessarily a body check. Sometimes the best return point is external information. Choose the anchor from the task rather than adding a complicated routine because it sounds professional.

## Plan the return
Use the sentence, “When I notice ___, I will return to ___, then ___.” The first part identifies a signal. The second selects the anchor. The third connects attention to action. For example, “When I start replaying the last error, I will look at the agreed entry mark, count in and begin the next phrase.”

The plan must allow flexibility. A usual visual anchor may not be available in a different room. Identify an alternative that serves the same purpose. Test the cue during appropriate practice and review whether it made the action clearer. Do not claim success merely because the phrase was repeated.
lessons.worked:
Jordan considers “commit” and “see the rim target.” The first supports effort. The second directs attention to specific external information. Jordan's stated problem is looking toward a spectator before shooting, so the target cue is a better first match for this case.

The anchor is the chosen part of the rim, not the word alone. After finding it, Jordan follows the practised setup. If Jordan has not learned the setup, the plan also needs instruction; repeating the cue is not enough.
lessons.application: Choose a cue and anchor for the next action. Explain why they fit this task.
lessons.label: Choose a usable return point
expected: Give one instructional and one motivational example.
Select the example that fits the stated need.
Name the anchor, trigger and next action.

checks.prompt: A cue reminds a singer to enter on the agreed count. What is its main purpose?
choices: Instructional: directing timing.
Motivational: raising effort regardless of timing.
Diagnostic: measuring anxiety.
checks.feedback: The cue directs a specific timing feature. It does not measure an internal state.

checks.prompt: The usual speaking card is unavailable. What is the most useful adjustment?
choices: Assume the presentation cannot be attempted.
Choose another brief anchor for the same main idea.
Add every remembered correction to the opening cue.
checks.feedback: The anchor serves a function. Another concise reminder can serve that function without turning the routine into a long instruction list.

lessons.support: A cue is what reminds you; an anchor is the return point you choose. They may overlap. State when the cue is used, what it means and what happens next. Short language is useful only when it connects to a clear task.

lessons.title: Prepare your attention
lessons.intro: Build a short sequence that connects preparation to the first action.
lessons.goal: I can explain the purpose of each step in a before-performance routine.
lessons.before: Use an existing skill and a realistic amount of preparation time.
lessons.core:
## A routine organizes attention
A **preperformance routine** is a planned sequence used before an action. It can include checking the task, choosing a cue and preparing to begin. Its purpose is to make the next action clearer. Completing a routine does not guarantee a successful outcome or require every nervous feeling to disappear.

Keep the routine suited to the setting. A free throw provides a different pause from a moving team play. A classroom presentation may allow a short check before speaking. A musical entry may need immediate attention to a conductor. A routine that takes too long can interfere with the task it is meant to support.

## Begin with information and preparation
First identify what the performer must know. Where is the action taking place? What is the starting cue? Is a rule or instruction unclear? Clarifying a task can be more useful than repeating a motivational phrase over missing information.

Preparation also includes skills and materials. A presenter checks that the needed example is ready. A player knows the agreed setup. A musician has practised the entry. Mental preparation works with those resources; it does not replace them.

## Give each step one job
A simple routine might have three parts: prepare, direct and begin. During preparation, the performer checks the task and uses any familiar, comfortable settling action that is useful. During direction, they choose the relevant cue. During beginning, they commit to the next practised action.

The names matter less than the purpose. Explain what each step directs attention toward. “Prepare” is too broad without a detail. “Check the starting position and listen for the official's signal” is a task-based instruction.

## Use a complete fictional example
For a school presentation, the routine could be: check the graph and speaking order; recall the cue “main relationship”; look toward the audience and begin the practised opening. The student may still feel uncertain. The sequence provides an action without demanding a perfect feeling first.

For sport, a brief body check belongs only at a suitable pause. Do not add breathing drills during swimming, active play or another task needing full attention. Describing a routine in writing is an acceptable way to demonstrate its purpose in this preview.

## Practise and revise the routine
A routine becomes more usable when its steps are understood and rehearsed. Try a hypothetical walkthrough or an appropriately supervised practice. Observe whether the sequence fits the available time and whether the final cue belongs to the task.

Record the routine separately from the result. One successful attempt does not prove that the routine caused success. One mistake does not automatically make the routine useless. Use specific observations to choose a sensible adjustment.
lessons.worked:
Jordan's routine is: check the line and starting position; briefly release unnecessary shoulder tension during the pause; find the rim target, use “smooth” and shoot. Each step has a purpose. The final attention is on the target and familiar action, not on continually checking feelings.

A teammate uses a different routine. That is not a problem if it fits their task. The assignment asks Jordan to explain and adapt the chosen sequence, not prove there is one correct ritual for everybody.
lessons.application: Build a short before-performance sequence. State what each step directs attention toward.
lessons.label: Prepare a short routine
expected: State the setting and available pause.
Give a labelled sequence with a purpose for each step.
Explain how the final step begins the task.

checks.prompt: What is the main purpose of a preperformance routine?
choices: Guarantee a particular result.
Remove all uncertainty before action.
Organize preparation and attention for the next task.
checks.feedback: A routine gives the performer useful actions. The result can still vary and some uncertainty may remain.

checks.prompt: The available preparation time is much shorter than usual. What should the performer do?
choices: Keep the essential task cue and adapt the sequence to the setting.
Insist on every usual step even if the task has begun.
Replace preparation with a claim of total confidence.
checks.feedback: A usable routine fits the available moment. Preserve its purpose while adjusting unnecessary steps.

lessons.support: Read the routine aloud. Could the performer tell when it begins, what each step does and when it ends? Remove steps without a purpose. Keep preparation, a useful cue and the next action connected.

lessons.title: Notice, reset and return
lessons.intro: Use a disruption as a signal for a practical next response.
lessons.goal: I can write an adaptable if–then plan that returns attention to useful information.
lessons.before: A reset ends with the task; it is not an endless check of feelings.
lessons.core:
## Disruption is part of a changing task
A performer may hear an unexpected sound, miss an entry or receive a new instruction. A **reset** is a brief response that helps them return to useful information. It does not erase the event. It creates a bridge from what happened to what the next action needs.

Start with a specific signal. “I am losing focus” is broad. “I keep replaying the last pass and have stopped checking teammates” identifies the pattern more clearly. A useful signal can be noticed without judging the whole person.

## Use an if–then plan
An **if–then plan** links a likely event to a response. “If the speaking order changes, then I will confirm when I begin and use my opening cue” is practical. It names both a trigger and an action.

Avoid trying to predict every possible problem. Choose a likely disruption that fits the case. Explain what the performer will do and what information they will attend to next. The response should be brief enough for the setting and should not create a new safety problem.

## Notice, adjust, return
One useful sequence is: notice the signal; make a proportionate adjustment during a suitable pause; return to the next task cue. A familiar comfortable breath, release of unnecessary tension or brief cue may be part of the adjustment. None is compulsory for every performer.

The goal is not to force calmness. Do not hold or force the breath, and stop a physical practice if uncomfortable. A written walkthrough is always available. A performer in active play may need to return directly to the relevant external information rather than begin an internal exercise.

## When the first response does not fit
A plan should include a check. Did the instruction become clearer? Can the performer identify the next cue? If not, another response may be needed. An unclear role may require a question. An unsafe demand requires a change or appropriate support, not more self-talk.

A reset also differs from denying an error. Useful feedback can be reviewed at a suitable break. The performer does not need to rehearse a whole technical analysis while the next attempt is starting. Separate immediate refocusing from later learning.

## Apply the sequence beyond sport
A musician who loses a count may listen for the next agreed entry cue. A student interrupted during a presentation may pause, identify the last completed point and return to the main claim. A recreational participant may ask for the instruction again. The wording changes, but the structure remains connected to the demand.

Judge the plan by its fit, clarity and flexibility. A successful reset is not defined by the learner claiming that every distracting thought disappeared.
lessons.worked:
The coach changes the drill order before Jordan's turn. Jordan is unsure whether to shoot or join the passing line. The appropriate first move is to clarify the new instruction. A breathing cue would not supply that missing information.

After clarification, Jordan selects the next task cue and begins. The if–then plan is: “If the drill order changes and my role is unclear, then I will ask where to begin, identify the next cue and rejoin the task.”
lessons.application: A disruption occurs. Describe the signal, your reset, and what you attend to next.
lessons.label: Write an if–then reset
expected: Name the disruption and observable signal.
Choose a safe, proportionate response.
State the next cue and an adjustment if the first response does not help.

checks.prompt: Which statement is a usable if–then plan?
choices: If I miss the entry, then I will find the next agreed cue and rejoin there.
If I feel uncertain, then the performance is already lost.
If anything changes, then I will repeat every preparation step.
checks.feedback: The plan names a specific event, an appropriate return cue and a next action. It can be practised and adapted.

checks.prompt: A learner cannot follow the next drill because the instruction is unclear. What fits first?
choices: Assume the learner lacks discipline.
Ask for clarification before choosing the next action.
Use a louder cue without checking the task.
checks.feedback: The problem is missing information. Clarification directly addresses it; a regulation cue does not replace instructions.

lessons.support: A reset has an exit. Write the last step first: what will the performer attend to or do next? Then choose the smallest appropriate adjustment that helps reach that action. Add a support request when the problem cannot be solved by attention alone.

lessons.title: Practise a flexible focus plan
lessons.intro: Use evidence and one changed condition to refine a plan.
lessons.goal: I can propose a suitable variation and explain what evidence would guide an adjustment.
lessons.before: Keep practice hypothetical or appropriately supervised; it is not a punishment.
lessons.core:
## A plan should travel beyond one familiar setting
A focus plan may work in a quiet practice and need adjusting in another setting. The useful question is not, “Can I force the same feeling everywhere?” It is, “Which information and actions still fit, and which need to change?”

**Flexible focus** means adapting attention to the task while keeping a clear purpose. It does not mean changing every cue after one mistake. Use evidence to decide which part of the plan needs attention.

## Change one condition deliberately
A hypothetical practice can vary the order of turns, the location of a visual cue or the amount of preparation time. Choose a change related to a likely performance demand. State what remains the same so the comparison is understandable.

For actual practice, use appropriate teacher or coach guidance. The variation should not involve humiliation, unsafe distraction or exhaustion as a test of character. You can demonstrate the reasoning through a written case or walkthrough without creating real pressure.

## Observe the action before interpreting it
Record what the performer intended to notice and what they actually did. For example: “Jordan looked toward the spectator after the missed shot and did not see the signal.” That observation is more useful than “Jordan has bad focus.”

Then consider possible explanations. Was the signal clear? Had the drill changed? Was Jordan replaying the error? A scenario may provide evidence for one explanation, but a single missed cue does not establish every cause. A strong response identifies both the evidence and its limits.

## Decide what to keep and what to adjust
Keep parts of the routine that still serve the task. Adjust the part affected by the changed condition. If the usual visual anchor is hidden, choose another relevant anchor. If the next action is unclear, clarify it rather than simply using the same cue more intensely.

A useful review includes a reason. “I would change the anchor because the usual marker is no longer visible” links the adjustment to evidence. “I would change everything because the attempt missed” makes a much larger claim than the result supports.

## Bring the phase together
Your plan should connect the demand, relevant information, attention shifts, cues and a disruption response. It should also distinguish learning-time analysis from a short cue during a familiar attempt. Preparation and feedback remain important even when the performer uses a refocus routine.

In Build, you will use one case to make that connection. In the unfamiliar transfer task, you will keep the useful principles while changing the details. The aim is an explanation that can adapt—not a memorized phrase that only fits one exact question.
lessons.worked_title: Keep the purpose; change the anchor
lessons.worked:
A presenter normally uses a highlighted word on a slide as an anchor. In a different room, the display is unavailable. The presenter can use the same key word on a speaking card, then explain the main relationship aloud.

The purpose remains directing attention to the main idea. The representation changes because the usual cue is unavailable. A useful observation is whether the speaker can resume the explanation, not whether they claim to feel exactly as they did in the original room.
lessons.application: Change one condition in a hypothetical practice. What would you observe before deciding whether the plan needs changing?
lessons.label: Test a focus plan thoughtfully
expected: Name one changed condition and what stays the same.
State the intended focus and an observable action.
Explain a proportionate adjustment and one uncertainty.

checks.prompt: What is a useful observation for reviewing a focus plan?
choices: The performer is definitely a low-focus person.
The performer looked at the agreed entry cue before beginning.
The game score proves the performer entered flow.
checks.feedback: The statement describes an action that can be checked. It does not claim a permanent trait or an unmeasured internal state.

checks.prompt: A cue is missed after a change in drill order. Which review is strongest?
choices: Treat the miss as proof that the whole routine failed.
Ignore the changed instruction and use more effort.
Check the instruction, the signal and what the performer attended to before revising one part.
checks.feedback: The review considers the task and competing explanations. It supports a targeted adjustment rather than an unsupported global conclusion.

lessons.support: Use four lines: intended cue, actual observation, possible explanation, next adjustment. Keep an uncertainty when the evidence does not settle the cause. A plan is flexible when it changes for a reason, not whenever a result disappoints.

labs.title: The next pass
labs.text: During open play, Jordan watches the basket but misses a teammate moving into clear space. Jordan says, “I was only thinking about shooting.” The next task is choosing a pass.
choices: Scan the ball, defenders and available teammates.
Keep attention only on the basket.
Review every previous mistake before passing.
labs.feedback: The case supplies both the missed information and Jordan’s account. A broad-external scan fits the passing decision. It would not be the same focus as a free throw.

labs.title: After a late entry
labs.text: A singer enters late and thinks, “I am terrible at performing.” The rehearsal leader says the agreed starting count was skipped. The next phrase has a clear entry cue.
choices: Deny that the entry was late.
Describe the skipped count, return to the next entry cue and review the count later.
Treat the mistake as evidence of permanent inability.
labs.feedback: Keep the useful observation and correction. A global judgment does not guide the next phrase. The response joins immediate refocusing with later practice.

labs.title: The display stops
labs.text: A student is about to explain a graph, but the display stops working. A printed copy is available and the teacher permits its use. The original anchor was a highlighted slide title.
choices: Wait for complete confidence before speaking.
Repeat the same visual routine while staring at the blank screen.
Use the printed graph as an anchor and adapt the opening cue.
labs.feedback: The task still needs an explanation of the graph. An available representation can support it. Changing the anchor preserves the purpose without requiring the original display.

lab_transfer: Choose a new sport, academic or artistic situation. Identify a changed demand, the attention it needs and a cue that fits. Explain one observation that would make you adjust the plan.

steps.title: Read the situation
steps.intro: Use Jordan or another clearly described fictional performer. Separate the task from your explanation of the difficulty.

fields.label: Task and changing demand
fields.help: Describe the performer, task and one moment when the information needed changes.
fields.example: Jordan needs a broad scan during open play and a precise target at the free-throw line.

fields.label: Distractions and evidence
fields.help: Identify an internal and an external distraction. Explain the evidence, rather than assuming a cause.
fields.example: Replaying the miss is internal. Watching a spectator is external. Jordan’s account connects these to the missed signal.

steps.title: Move attention
steps.intro: Give width and direction, then explain why they fit the task.

fields.label: Useful focus now
fields.help: Choose the appropriate focus at one stated moment and justify it.
fields.example: Before the pass, broad-external attention includes available teammates and defenders.

fields.label: Three moments and their triggers
fields.help: Describe at least three moments, their information needs and what triggers each shift.
fields.example: Open play: scan teammates. Whistle: listen to the official. Free throw: find the chosen rim target.

steps.title: Prepare a routine
steps.intro: A cue and an anchor are useful when their purpose is clear. Keep the routine short.

fields.label: Cue examples and selection
fields.help: Give one instructional and one motivational cue. Select one for the case and explain why.
fields.example: “See the target” directs attention; “commit” supports effort. Jordan first needs the target cue.

fields.label: Anchor and use
fields.help: Name a return point, when it is used and the next action.
fields.example: At the line, the rim target is the anchor. Jordan finds it before following the familiar setup.

fields.label: Before-performance sequence
fields.help: Write a labelled sequence. Explain what each part directs attention toward.
fields.example: Prepare: check the starting position. Direct: find the target and use “smooth.” Begin: take the practised shot.

steps.title: Plan a disruption
steps.intro: Use a realistic interruption. A hypothetical walkthrough is sufficient.

fields.label: Disruption and response
fields.help: Name the signal, response and next task cue. Include clarification when instructions are missing.
fields.example: If the drill order changes and the role is unclear, ask where to begin, then identify the next cue.

fields.label: Walkthrough with a changed demand
fields.help: Describe one appropriate variation, what stays the same and what the performer would observe.
fields.example: In a hypothetical practice, shorten the preparation pause. Keep the task the same and check whether the essential target cue is still used.

steps.title: Review and transfer
steps.intro: Use an observation, not a game score, to explain the plan.

fields.label: Observation and adjustment
fields.help: Describe a factual observation and one adjustment it could support. Label invented observations as hypothetical.
fields.example: Hypothetically, Jordan looks away before the signal. Review the trigger for returning to the target rather than label Jordan as unfocused.

fields.label: Adapt to an unfamiliar task
fields.help: New case: a musician is moved from a solo to a duet. Explain a changed focus, a useful cue and a disruption response.
fields.example: The duet adds a partner’s timing cue. Plan a shared entry and return point rather than using the solo routine unchanged.

fields.label: Why attention must change
fields.help: Justify one transition in your plan and explain one limit of what your evidence can show.
fields.example: The passing decision needs several external cues, while a free throw uses a precise target. One missed cue does not identify every possible cause.

reviews.prompt: Explain how broad/narrow attention differs from internal/external attention. Use one example.
reviews.answer: Width concerns how much information is selected; direction concerns where it comes from. A player scanning several teammates is broad-external. A brief check of one tension signal during a pause is narrow-internal. The task determines whether either fits.

reviews.prompt: A familiar cue becomes unavailable before a presentation. Explain a useful response.
reviews.answer: Identify the purpose of the cue and choose an available alternative serving that purpose. A printed keyword may replace a slide title. Explain the next action and check whether the new anchor makes the explanation usable.

reviews.prompt: Correct this claim: “The Inner Game equation calculates potential, and Self 1 and Self 2 are separate brain systems.”
reviews.answer: Gallwey’s equation is an attributed coaching framework, not a measurement. Self 1 and Self 2 are labels for discussing commentary and learned execution. The framework does not replace skill learning, task knowledge or useful feedback.

reviews.prompt: Revisit one lesson response. Describe one useful revision and why it improves your focus plan.
reviews.answer: A useful revision replaces vague language with a specific task, cue, trigger or observation. For example, “focus more” can become a named scan before a pass. Explain the change and retain a limitation where the evidence does not establish a cause.

checkpoint.prompt: A student selects the graph’s main relationship, stays with it and shifts to a relevant question. What does this show?
choices: Attention involves selecting, sustaining and shifting according to the task.
Concentration requires one unchanging cue throughout.
Every available detail deserves equal attention.
Attention can only be directed to physical movement.
checkpoint.feedback: The task changes from explaining to responding. Selection, sustained attention and a purposeful shift work together.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can a long list of corrections be unhelpful during a familiar action?
choices: All technical thinking is harmful in every setting.
Competing instructions can exceed what is useful in that moment.
A learned skill needs no further feedback.
Short cues automatically guarantee success.
checkpoint.feedback: The issue is competing jobs in a specific moment. Learning-time analysis and later feedback remain important.

checkpoint.prompt: A player scans defenders, teammates and open space before passing. Which quadrant fits?
choices: Narrow-internal.
Broad-internal.
Broad-external.
Narrow-external.
checkpoint.feedback: Several relevant cues in the surroundings make this broad-external attention.

checkpoint.prompt: During a safe pause, a singer briefly checks one area of jaw tension. Which quadrant fits this moment?
choices: Broad-external.
Broad-internal.
Narrow-external.
Narrow-internal.
checkpoint.feedback: The selected information is one specific bodily sensation. That describes narrow-internal attention.

checkpoint.prompt: How is Gallwey’s performance equation used here?
choices: As a coaching framework for discussing interference.
As a calculation of a student’s hidden potential.
As a formula proving the cause of every error.
As a replacement for learning a skill.
checkpoint.feedback: It organizes a discussion. It does not supply measured values or remove other influences on performance.

checkpoint.prompt: What do Self 1 and Self 2 name in the attributed framework?
choices: Two separate anatomical brain structures.
The judging/telling role and learned execution.
Two fixed classes of athlete.
A diagnostic score and its treatment.
checkpoint.feedback: These are model labels, not anatomy, diagnoses or permanent learner categories.

checkpoint.prompt: Which statement keeps useful information without judging the whole person?
choices: I never make mistakes.
I am not a performer.
My setup was rushed; I will use the agreed cue and review it.
The miss proves the routine can never work.
checkpoint.feedback: A specific observation supports a next action without denying the error or making a global claim.

checkpoint.prompt: A useful preperformance routine should primarily…
choices: require an identical sequence in every environment.
wait for every nervous feeling to disappear.
replace technical preparation.
connect preparation, a task cue and the next action.
checkpoint.feedback: The sequence must fit the task and available time. It supports, rather than replaces, preparation.

checkpoint.prompt: The usual visual anchor is hidden in a new room. What fits an adaptable what-if plan?
choices: Choose another cue serving the same task purpose.
Abandon the performance automatically.
Repeat the old sequence without checking the environment.
Treat the missing cue as a test of personal worth.
checkpoint.feedback: Adapt the representation while preserving the purpose of the anchor.

checkpoint.prompt: Which pairing correctly distinguishes cue purposes?
choices: “Keep going” always teaches a specific movement; “see the target” only raises effort.
“See the target” can be instructional; “commit” can support effort.
All short phrases have the same purpose.
Motivational cues measure bodily activation.
checkpoint.feedback: Purpose and context determine the distinction. A phrase is not useful merely because it is short.

checkpoint.prompt: A distracting thought returns during a familiar task. Which response fits this phase?
choices: Require the thought to disappear before acting.
Use the game score to diagnose attention.
Notice the drift and return to a relevant cue when appropriate.
Ignore useful external information to monitor every thought.
checkpoint.feedback: The aim is a task-based return, not perfect control of every thought. Real problems may need clarification or support.

checkpoint.prompt: Jordan missed a free throw after a rushed setup, then watched a spectator instead of the next signal. Which plan best fits the stated evidence?
choices: Assume every miss proves low ability.
Use the same narrow focus during all open play.
Remove feedback to prevent any analysis.
Use the familiar setup and target cue, then shift to the signal for the next task.
checkpoint.feedback: The case identifies a rushed setup and a later attention shift that did not fit the task. The plan addresses both without claiming those facts explain every possible miss.

glossary.Attention: Selecting and using information for a task.
glossary.Concentration: Sustaining attention with information that matters.
glossary.Task-relevant: Useful for the action or decision currently needed.
glossary.Distraction: Information that competes with the current task.
glossary.Broad attention: Considering several relevant pieces of information.
glossary.Internal attention: Attention to thoughts or bodily sensations.
glossary.External attention: Attention to information in the surroundings.
glossary.Attention shift: A change in the information selected when the demand changes.
glossary.Nonjudgmental observation: A factual description without a verdict on personal worth.
glossary.Inner Game: Gallwey’s attributed coaching framework for discussing learned execution and interference.
glossary.Self 1 / Self 2: Model labels for commentary and learned execution, not brain structures.
glossary.Instructional cue: A brief reminder directing technique, timing or information.
glossary.Motivational cue: A brief reminder supporting effort or commitment.
glossary.Anchor: A chosen return point for attention.
glossary.Preperformance routine: A planned sequence connecting preparation to the next action.
glossary.If–then plan: A stated disruption linked to a practical response.
glossary.Reset: A proportionate response ending with a useful task cue.
glossary.Practice variation: A planned, appropriate change in a practice condition.
glossary.Transfer: Adapting an idea to a different task or condition.
